title: Mapping the Cortex: Areas and Arealization

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The cerebral cortex is a sheet of {{c1::neurons}} on the surface of the forebrain.
cards.quote: The cerebral cortex is the sheet of neurons on the surface of the forebrain.

cards.front: What is cortical arealization?
cards.back: The process that establishes distinct cortical areas, each with its own inputs, outputs and functions.
cards.quote: Each area has its own inputs and outputs, and many sensory areas hold an internal map of the body or the world.

cards.front: In a mouse hemisphere, what is the front-to-back order of motor, visual and somatosensory cortex?
cards.back: Motor at the front, somatosensory in the middle, visual at the back.
cards.quote: Motor cortex sits at the front. Somatosensory cortex, the touch area, sits in the middle.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: What is the thalamus’s role in sensory pathways to cortex?
cards.back: It relays signals from the eyes, ears and skin to the cortex.
cards.quote: the relay station that passes signals from the eyes, ears and skin to the cortex
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: Why does the mouse developmental timeline allow a cortical map to begin independently of thalamic input?
cards.back: The sheet is already patterned and producing neurons before thalamic axons arrive; those axons enter the cortical plate later, around birth.
cards.quote: So the sheet is already patterned and making neurons before the thalamic axons arrive.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: Proteins that switch genes on or off are called {{c1::transcription factors}}.
cards.quote: transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on or off
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: Removing a developmental factor shifts a border, but adding more produces no detectable shift. Does the failed gain experiment exclude a role in positioning, and why?
cards.back: No. Redundancy or buffering can conceal the gain response, so a missing converse effect does not exclude a role.
cards.quote: A missing converse result does not rule a factor out, since redundancy or buffering can hide it.
cards.section: The layout

cards.front: How do protomap and protocortex differ about the origin of cortical area identity?
cards.back: Protomap places the initial positional bias in progenitors. Protocortex gives young cortex broadly similar potential, with incoming thalamic axons mainly determining area identity.
cards.quote: Here the young cortex is a sheet with broadly similar potential, and areas emerge mainly from the axons that arrive from the thalamus.
cards.section: Two answers, and what each predicts

cards.front: How can a patch of cortical progenitors give rise to a column of neurons above it?
cards.back: Newborn neurons migrate outward along radial glia, so neurons born from one ventricular-zone patch stack above that patch.
cards.quote: newborn neurons climb outward along radial glia, long scaffold cells that span the wall.
cards.section: Two answers, and what each predicts

cards.front: Why does a shifted cortical marker-gene border at birth establish less than a shifted adult functional area?
cards.back: It establishes a change in a molecular proxy for future areas. Mature borders and function require later measurements.
cards.quote: Some genes have expression borders at birth that line up with future areas.
cards.section: Reading a map in a newborn

cards.front: Dye placed in a newborn cortical spot labels neurons in a thalamic nucleus associated with visual input. What can this readout tell you about that spot?
cards.back: It has connections consistent with visual cortex. The dye identifies thalamic neurons projecting to the injected spot; it does not by itself establish adult visual function.
cards.quote: Dye placed in one spot of cortex labels the thalamic neurons that project there, sometimes in more than one nucleus,
cards.section: Reading a map in a newborn

cards.front: In rodent somatosensory cortex, whisker-related cell clusters called barrels occupy layer {{c1::4}}.
cards.quote: In layer 4 of rodent somatosensory cortex, clusters of cells called barrels, one for each large whisker,
cards.section: Reading a map in a newborn

cards.front: What perturbation tests whether a signal is necessary for a developmental structure or its position?
cards.back: Remove or block the signal, then look for loss or displacement of the structure.
cards.quote: A test of whether it is necessary: remove or block it and look for the loss or shift of what it controls.
cards.section: A lamp at the front: FGF8

cards.front: Adding a signal at a new site and inducing a structure there tests {{c1::sufficiency}}.
cards.quote: add it where it is normally absent, or add more of it, and look for a structure induced, enlarged or moved.
cards.section: A lamp at the front: FGF8

cards.front: In a hypothetical developing tissue, a signal decreases from front to back and a border forms at a fixed signal threshold. The signal rises everywhere but still decreases backward. What happens to the border, and why?
cards.back: It moves toward the back, if the threshold is still crossed on the tissue. The old border now has too much signal; the threshold is reached farther back.
cards.quote: Under a brighter lamp, cells read themselves as farther forward than they are, so each border falls farther back.
cards.section: A lamp at the front: FGF8

cards.front: FGF8 production is increased at the normal front source in the mouse cortical primordium. What happens to the barrel field, and why?
cards.back: It shifts toward the back. Higher FGF8 makes progenitors read their positions as farther forward, moving the borders backward.
cards.quote: Under a brighter lamp, cells read themselves as farther forward than they are, so each border falls farther back.
cards.section: A lamp at the front: FGF8

cards.front: An extra FGF8 source at the back of mouse embryonic cortex induces a partial second barrel field behind the normal one. What causal claim does this support?
cards.back: An extra FGF8 source is sufficient to induce part of a repeated area pattern. It does not establish that every area will duplicate.
cards.quote: An extra source inducing an extra area is a test of sufficiency.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An FGF-binding blocker is placed at the front of the mouse cortical primordium. What happens to the barrel field, and why?
cards.back: It shifts toward the front. Reduced FGF signalling makes anterior cells read themselves as farther back; front territories should shrink and posterior ones expand forward.
cards.quote: the front areas should shrink and the posterior areas expand forward; the barrel field moved toward the front.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A developmental inhibitor shifts a border but binds both the intended signal and related signals. Can this result alone establish that the intended signal is uniquely necessary?
cards.back: No. The necessity rule links loss of signalling to the shift, but the inhibitor’s shared targets prevent attribution to one signal. A perturbation that isolates the intended signal would distinguish them.
cards.quote: which binds FGF8, and probably related FGFs, before they reach the cells.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a hypothetical 5.0 mm cortex, a mapped border is 2.1 mm from the front before a perturbation and 1.5 mm afterward. What percentage of cortical length did it move, and in which direction?
cards.back: Displacement = 1.5 − 2.1 = −0.6 mm, where distance increases toward the back. Fraction = 0.6/5.0 = 0.12: 12% of cortical length toward the front.
cards.quote: the barrel field moved toward the front. That is a test of necessity.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: For the illustrative cortical gradient C = C₀e^(−x/λ), the position of threshold T is x = {{c1::λ ln(C₀/T)}}.
cards.quote: A border sits where the level equals that border's threshold T, at x = λ ln(C₀/T).
cards.section: How far does a border move?

cards.front: In the illustrative exponential cortical model, λ = L/5 and a border starts at x = 0.50L. Double C₀ while keeping λ and T fixed. Where does the border move?
cards.back: Δx = λ ln 2 = (L/5) ln 2 ≈ 0.139L toward the back. New x = 0.50L + 0.139L ≈ 0.64L, measured from the front.
cards.quote: every border that stays on the sheet moves back by the same distance, λ ln 2, about 0.7 decay lengths,
cards.section: How far does a border move?

cards.front: Why does doubling the source shift all retained borders equally in the illustrative exponential cortical model?
cards.back: With λ and thresholds fixed, x = λ ln(C₀/T). Doubling C₀ adds λ ln 2, independent of the threshold.
cards.quote: because ln(2C₀/T) = ln(C₀/T) + ln 2 whatever the threshold.
cards.section: How far does a border move?

cards.front: In the illustrative exponential cortical model, the source is halved while λ and thresholds stay fixed. Two internal borders remain on the sheet. What happens to the width of the band between them, and why?
cards.back: Its width stays the same. Both borders shift forward by the same distance, λ ln 2, so their separation is unchanged.
cards.quote: The bands between A and C keep their width; the front band grows and the back band shrinks, or the reverse.
cards.section: How far does a border move?

cards.front: Where are Emx2 and Pax6 highest in the mouse cortical progenitor sheet?
cards.back: Emx2: back and medial. Pax6: front and lateral.
cards.quote: Emx2 is highest at the back. Pax6 is highest at the front.
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: Which mouse cortical progenitor factors complement Emx2 and Pax6 by peaking back/lateral and front/medial, respectively?
cards.back: COUP-TFI peaks back/lateral; Sp8 peaks front/medial.
cards.quote: Each also varies from the midline outward, and two more factors join them:
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: Emx2 is deleted in mouse cortical development. What shift is expected in area markers at birth, and why?
cards.back: Motor and somatosensory territories expand backward, while visual territory shrinks. Removing a factor highest posteriorly weakens the progenitors’ record of posterior position.
cards.quote: the front-and-middle areas, motor and somatosensory, grow toward the back and the visual area shrinks.
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: In mice, Emx2 loss shrinks visual territory. Raising Emx2 while preserving its slope enlarges visual territory without significantly changing total cortical area. Why does combining these results favor territory allocation over a simple growth requirement?
cards.back: Opposite map shifts support territory allocation, while no significant total-size change in the gain experiment argues against a simple growth effect. This uses the reciprocal-perturbation rule and the growth control; it does not require Emx2 to act independently of every other signal.
cards.quote: the visual area grew and the front areas shrank, with no significant change in the total area of cortex.
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: A mouse lacks working Pax6 throughout development. What area-marker shift is reported near birth, and why should it be called a marker result?
cards.back: Front territories shrink and visual territory expands forward. The readout precedes mature areas and does not by itself establish adult functional borders.
cards.quote: the front areas shrank and the visual area expanded forward.
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: COUP-TFI is deleted only from mouse cortex. What happens to motor and sensory territories, and why?
cards.back: Motor territories spread and sensory territories are squeezed toward the back. Cortical COUP-TFI is needed to preserve sensory territory.
cards.quote: removed it from cortex alone, in a conditional knockout (a gene deleted only in chosen cells), and the sensory areas were squeezed toward the back
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: Why is Pax6’s role in positioning mouse cortical areas less settled than Emx2’s?
cards.back: Pax6 gain barely shifts the map, and cortical loss can shift markers without shifting thalamic connections. Later results differ, so the evidence is mixed.
cards.quote: Pax6 is the cautionary case: its gain does not mirror its loss.
cards.section: The cells' own record of position

cards.front: Gbx2-mutant mice lack thalamic axons reaching cortex but retain several normal area-marker borders at birth. What does this establish, and what remains untested?
cards.back: The initial marker sketch can form without thalamic input, supporting protomap. These newborn markers do not establish that adult borders or function are input-independent.
cards.quote: The marker sketch forms without thalamic input.
cards.section: Input finishes the drawing

cards.front: Fetal rat visual cortex grafted into newborn somatosensory cortex receives whisker-related thalamic input and forms barrels. What does that show?
cards.back: Young cortex destined for vision can build a somatosensory feature under new input, supporting the input-dependent component of protocortex.
cards.quote: Tissue bound for visual cortex could still build a feature of another area when given that area's input.
cards.section: Input finishes the drawing

cards.front: What did orientation maps in adult ferret auditory cortex receiving rerouted visual input show about cortical organization?
cards.back: Input can shape an area’s internal organization. The rewired cortex formed a visual-like orientation map, though less regular than the visual cortex map.
cards.quote: arranged in a map like that of visual cortex, though less regular.
cards.section: Input finishes the drawing

cards.front: What did removing mouse visual-thalamic axons reveal about the distinction between primary and higher-order visual cortex?
cards.back: Their genetic distinction failed to develop, showing that thalamic input helps refine the cortical sketch into primary and higher-order areas.
cards.quote: the genetic distinction between primary visual cortex and the higher-order visual areas around it, which further process what primary visual cortex passes on, failed to develop.
cards.section: Input finishes the drawing

cards.front: How can normal newborn cortical markers without thalamic input coexist with barrels in grafted visual tissue receiving whisker input?
cards.back: The two-stage rule explains both: progenitors establish an initial positional sketch, while later input shapes the features an area builds. The experiments address different stages and readouts.
cards.quote: Input sharpens borders, separates primary from higher-order areas, and helps build the maps inside them
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: A perturbation shifts a newborn cortical marker border. A researcher claims it shifts an adult sensory function. What further observation would directly test that claim?
cards.back: Measure the adult functional boundary in surviving animals and compare controls. The readout rule distinguishes a marker pattern from function; a newborn proxy alone cannot establish the claimed adult effect.
cards.quote: The manipulations in this lesson test different things: a border's position, a marker pattern, connections, or a map inside an area.
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: A threshold model predicts where cortical area borders sit. Why does that prediction alone not explain maps within each area?
cards.back: Border position and internal organization are different outcomes. Internal maps also depend on input and activity interacting with cortical cells.
cards.quote: Its threshold model does not explain the maps inside an area, such as barrels and orientation modules; those depend on input and activity
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: Activating the fly gene eyeless at abnormal sites produces eyes on legs and wings. What does this show, and why does it not settle Pax6’s cortical role?
cards.back: It demonstrates sufficiency for ectopic eye formation in that context. Sufficiency for eyes does not establish how Pax6 positions areas within existing cortex.
cards.quote: flies grew eyes on their legs and wings. That is sufficiency in its starkest form.
cards.section: Pax6, the eye gene

cards.front: Is Emx2’s influence on cortical arealization established to operate exclusively through FGF signalling?
cards.back: No. One group proposed FGF regulation; another raised Emx2 without changing Fgf8 and argued for direct progenitor effects. Both routes may contribute.
cards.quote: when they raised Emx2 in progenitors, Fgf8 did not change, and they argued that Emx2 acts on the progenitors directly.
cards.section: Does Emx2 act through FGF signalling?

cards.front: In a hypothetical cortex, a mutant has a smaller sensory area than a control. What additional size comparison helps distinguish general growth failure from territory reallocation?
cards.back: Compare total cortical area and relative area shares. Smaller total size with preserved shares is compatible with general growth failure; changed shares at unchanged total size support reallocation. This uses the growth-versus-allocation distinction.
cards.quote: several of these factors also change progenitor proliferation.
cards.section: A shifted map, or a smaller sheet?

cards.front: In the illustrative linear cortical model C = C₀(1 − x/L), a border starts at x = 0.25L. Halve C₀ from its normal value while keeping the threshold fixed. Where is the predicted crossing?
cards.back: Initially T = 0.75C₀. After halving: 0.75C₀ = 0.5C₀(1 − x/L), so x/L = −0.50. The formal crossing moves forward by 0.75L, beyond the front; the border is lost from the sheet.
cards.quote: That would push border A off the sheet (to −0.5) and park border B exactly at the front edge.
cards.section: What the threshold model does and does not say

cards.front: Two cortical threshold models use identical fixed thresholds but different decreasing profiles: exponential or linear. Which prediction survives a stronger source, and which prediction depends on the profile?
cards.back: Backward shifts survive, for crossings retained on the sheet. Equal displacement of all borders requires the exponential rule Δx = λ ln(factor); linear profiles give threshold-dependent shifts. The shared rule is crossing a fixed threshold on a decreasing profile.
cards.quote: A straight-line profile behaves differently. If the level falls as C = C₀(1 − x/L) across a sheet of length L,
cards.section: What the threshold model does and does not say

cards.front: In a two-source cortical threshold model, a new rear source raises a previously low central level and creates a rising profile near the rear. What can happen to low-level bands and the order of repeated bands, and why?
cards.back: Low-level bands can shrink or disappear; thresholds reached near the rear are crossed again in reverse order. This follows from additive source levels and threshold crossings, not a guarantee that every real cortical area duplicates.
cards.quote: Near the new source the level climbs again, and any threshold it reaches is crossed a second time, in reverse order.
cards.section: What the threshold model does and does not say
